label: 核心算子、融合 Kernel 与 Attention

questions.subtopic: Attention backward / Memory footprint and recomputation
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the peak activation memory of standard attention backward and how FlashAttention-style recomputation changes it.
questions.stem: Consider the backward pass of standard attention O = softmax(Q @ K^T / sqrt(d)) @ V for shapes Q, K, V ∈ [B, H, N, d]. Select all correct statements about activation memory and recomputation. (Choose all that apply.)
questions.codeSnippet:
# Forward:
# S = Q @ K^T / sqrt(d)                # [B, H, N, N]
# P = softmax(S, dim=-1)               # [B, H, N, N]
# O = P @ V                             # [B, H, N, d]

# Backward (given dO):
# Need dQ, dK, dV. Naive requires materialized P (or S).

options.text: FlashAttention avoids storing P in HBM by re-tiling backward: it stores only per-row (m, l) statistics from forward (size O(B*H*N)) and recomputes P block-by-block from Q, K in backward, trading extra compute for a large HBM saving.

In FlashAttention backward, the extra recomputation makes total FLOPs strictly larger than the forward-only baseline; the wall-clock speedup comes entirely from reduced HBM traffic dominating the extra compute.

The naive backward stores the softmax output P (or S) of shape [B, H, N, N] from forward and re-uses it in backward; this dominates activation memory for long sequences (quadratic in N) and is the main reason non-flash attention runs out of memory at long context.

The backward gradient of softmax with respect to logits requires access to the full P matrix element-by-element; there is no way to avoid materializing P in HBM at some point in any correct algorithm.

assumptions: Discussion is training attention with standard cross-entropy loss upstream.
'Naive backward' means a straightforward autograd derivation without I/O-aware fusion.

questions.subtopic: Convolution / Direct vs im2col-GEMM
questions.learningObjective: Compare direct convolution and im2col-based GEMM convolution in terms of memory and compute.
questions.stem: Compare two implementation strategies for a standard 2D convolution: (1) direct convolution kernel that computes each output pixel with its own R*S*C-tap sum; (2) im2col followed by cuBLAS/GEMM. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: Both have the same FLOP count. im2col replicates each input pixel R*S times into a lowered matrix (extra memory and HBM traffic), then calls a highly-tuned GEMM; direct convolution avoids the replication cost but requires a custom kernel with careful data reuse. im2col is often faster in practice because the GEMM tail leverages tensor cores well.
im2col strictly reduces FLOPs compared to direct convolution because it removes the redundant multiplications along the receptive field, converting the convolution into an equivalent smaller matmul.
Direct convolution stores overlapping receptive fields once in HBM and streams them per output; im2col requires strictly less memory because the reshaped matrix reuses input storage in place.
Both strategies have the same FLOPs, memory traffic, and peak memory; the choice is purely about kernel implementation complexity and does not affect end-to-end performance.

assumptions: Standard 2D convolution with stride >= 1 and non-trivial R, S.
im2col produces a [N*H_out*W_out, C*R*S] matrix multiplied by a [C*R*S, K] weight matrix.

questions.subtopic: Embedding lookup / Gather kernel
questions.learningObjective: Characterize the embedding lookup as a gather kernel and identify its memory access pattern.
questions.stem: The input embedding layer takes an int64 index tensor [B, N] and gathers rows from a weight table [V, D] (vocabulary V, hidden dim D). Which characterization of this kernel is correct?

options.text: It is a random-access read of individual elements: for each output element out[b, n, d] the kernel reads a single scalar table[idx[b,n], d], so global memory transactions are uncoalesced by design and the kernel is latency-bound.

It is functionally equivalent to a GEMM between a one-hot [B, N, V] input and the [V, D] table; a good implementation actually forms this one-hot and calls a sparse-GEMM primitive, which is faster than a hand-written gather kernel.
It is a reduction kernel that sums the embedding rows selected by all B*N indices; the output is [D] per batch item, and the runtime is dominated by the reduction depth log2(B*N).

It is a gather kernel with irregular but coalesced-per-row access: each of the B*N indices induces one contiguous read of D floats from the [V, D] table. FLOPs are zero; runtime is bandwidth-bound on the D-element rows read from the embedding table.

assumptions: Standard row-major embedding weight [V, D].
Warps cooperatively load a row rather than each thread choosing a different row.

questions.subtopic: GEMM epilogue fusion / Bias + activation + norm
questions.learningObjective: Reason about which operations can be fused as a GEMM epilogue and what the HBM-traffic benefit is.
questions.stem: A GEMM Y = X @ W is followed by (i) bias add, (ii) elementwise activation (GELU), (iii) RMSNorm along the last axis. Select all statements about fusing these into a GEMM epilogue that are correct. (Choose all that apply.)
questions.codeSnippet:
# Sequence to fuse:
# Y0 = X @ W                              # GEMM
# Y1 = Y0 + bias                          # (i) bias add, per-row broadcast
# Y2 = gelu(Y1)                           # (ii) elementwise activation
# Y3 = rmsnorm(Y2, gamma)                 # (iii) reduction across last axis + normalize

options.text: Fusing the epilogue removes tensor-core benefit because tensor cores can only accumulate into registers, and any epilogue instruction moves the accumulator to shared memory first, forcing a synchronous barrier that undoes the tensor-core throughput advantage.

(i) bias add and (ii) elementwise activation fuse naturally as a GEMM epilogue because they are pure elementwise transforms on the accumulator tile before it is written to HBM; the fused kernel avoids the intermediate Y0 and Y1 HBM roundtrips.

(iii) RMSNorm fuses as a standard GEMM epilogue in the same way as bias-add and activation, because normalization is elementwise once the running variance is precomputed as a scalar constant of the workload.

(iii) RMSNorm requires a reduction along the last axis (i.e., across the D_out output columns of the GEMM tile), which typically cuts across CTAs unless the GEMM is designed with a full-row tile; in mainstream libraries, RMSNorm is left as a separate kernel or fused only with a specialized 'GEMM-with-row-reduction' epilogue.

assumptions: Standard cuBLASLt / CUTLASS epilogue programming model applies.
GEMM tile size does not span the full D_out row of the output.

questions.subtopic: FFT / Custom operator characteristics
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the memory and compute characteristics of FFT and related transforms as custom operators inside ML models.
questions.stem: A model uses a 1D FFT of length N (with N a power of two) as a custom operator inside a layer. Select all correct statements about this operator on GPU. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: The Cooley-Tukey FFT has O(N log N) compute (versus O(N^2) for a naive DFT); on modern GPUs cuFFT organizes the computation into O(log N) rounds of butterfly operations, each round with a specific stride pattern that dominates its memory access.

FFT of length N reads/writes O(N) elements per round; the compute-to-byte ratio per round is essentially constant (small), which makes FFT of large N memory-bandwidth bound on GPU rather than compute bound.
Because FFT preserves L2 norms (Parseval), it introduces no numerical error and can therefore be treated as a bit-exact linear operator regardless of floating-point precision used.

In ML models, FFT is often used to accelerate long-range convolutions via the convolution theorem: conv(a, b) = IFFT(FFT(a) * FFT(b)); the crossover point where FFT-based convolution beats direct convolution grows with kernel size.

assumptions: N is a power of two so radix-2 or radix-4 FFTs apply directly.
GPU has HBM and standard cuFFT-like optimized implementations available.

questions.subtopic: FlashAttention / IO complexity and backward recomputation
questions.learningObjective: Explain FlashAttention's core algorithmic idea: block-tiled attention with online softmax and backward recomputation of the attention matrix.

requiredFeatures: large SMEM for K, V, S tiles

questions.stem: Which statement most accurately describes the algorithmic contribution of FlashAttention (as an exact attention algorithm)?

options.text: FlashAttention keeps the attention math exact but reorders the computation into K/V-block tiles with an online softmax so the full N x N attention matrix is never materialized in HBM; in the backward pass the attention weights are recomputed from stored (m, l) statistics and Q, K, V rather than reloaded from HBM.

FlashAttention replaces softmax with a low-rank approximation whose rank is chosen per tile, reducing attention from O(N^2) to O(N sqrt(N)) FLOPs while remaining within an epsilon-approximation of exact attention.

FlashAttention prunes tokens with attention weight below a learned threshold (sparse attention) and skips the corresponding tiles; correctness is preserved because the pruned weights are provably below numerical noise for typical language models.
FlashAttention rewrites attention in FP8 with per-row scale factors that let the softmax denominator be computed without dequantization; the FP8 arithmetic is the key to the wall-clock speedup.

assumptions: Discussion refers to FlashAttention v1/v2 exact attention (not FlashAttention-style approximate variants).
SMEM per SM is large enough to hold Q, K, V, and S tiles for the chosen block sizes.

questions.subtopic: FlashAttention / HBM traffic analysis of attention
questions.learningObjective: Compare HBM traffic patterns between naive attention (materialized S = QK^T) and FlashAttention (block-tiled, streamed).
questions.stem: Compare the HBM traffic of naive attention (which explicitly materializes S = QK^T in HBM before softmax and O = softmax(S)V) with FlashAttention over a single (B=1, H=1) head with sequence length N and head dim d = 64. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: Naive: O(N*d) reads/writes; FlashAttention: O(N^2) reads/writes. FlashAttention pays more HBM traffic in exchange for constant SMEM usage and lower peak register pressure.
Both algorithms have HBM traffic dominated by loading Q, K, V (O(N*d)) and writing O (O(N*d)); FlashAttention's benefit is entirely from fusing softmax into the matmul, not from I/O.
Both have HBM traffic O(N^2); FlashAttention only saves compute by fusing softmax with the K, V matmul into a single kernel.

Naive attention has HBM traffic dominated by writing and re-reading S (O(N^2)), on top of loading Q, K, V, and writing O. FlashAttention keeps S entirely on-chip and its HBM traffic is O(N^2 * d / M) where M is on-chip memory per SM, reducing to roughly O(N*d) when a full K/V tile fits — much less than naive for large N.

assumptions: Standard (non-fused) baseline actually writes S to HBM (as in an unoptimized softmax-then-matmul kernel).
The on-chip memory M is at least large enough to hold one Q tile and one K/V tile.

questions.subtopic: FlashAttention / Design properties and non-implications
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish claims about FlashAttention that are algorithm-level truths from common overgeneralizations about performance.
questions.stem: Select all statements about FlashAttention that are correct at the algorithm-and-analysis level (i.e., independent of any specific paper wall-clock number). (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: FlashAttention delivers a fixed wall-clock speedup (roughly 3-4x) uniformly across sequence lengths, batch sizes, and head dimensions on all modern GPUs, because it is designed to be independent of hardware configuration.

The backward pass of FlashAttention deliberately recomputes the softmax probabilities block-by-block from stored (m, l) statistics; this recomputation trades extra FLOPs for a much smaller HBM footprint.
FlashAttention is exact (bitwise up to summation-order rounding, not approximate) and does not change the FLOP count of forward attention.
FlashAttention's asymptotic HBM I/O scales as O(N^2 d / M), where M is on-chip memory per SM; the gap versus O(N^2) baselines grows with N.

assumptions: 'FlashAttention' refers to the FA v1/v2 exact algorithms.
'Wall-clock speedup' is shape and hardware dependent.

questions.subtopic: Fused MLP / Activation fusion boundary
questions.learningObjective: Reason about which parts of an MLP block can be fused into a single GPU kernel and where the fusion boundary lies for a Fused-QKV/-MLP style optimization.
questions.stem: A standard MLP block computes y = down(activation(up(x))) with intermediate size F. For x shape [B, N, D] and F > D, which fusion strategy is most consistent with how modern LLM inference kernels are structured?

options.text: Fuse up + activation into one kernel (writing intermediate a of shape [B, N, F] to HBM) and keep down as a separate GEMM. The [B, N, F] tensor is written and read once, which is acceptable because the down GEMM is a big matmul that would not fuse with an elementwise activation without hurting its tile design.

Fuse up + activation + down into a single kernel that never materializes the [B, N, F] intermediate in HBM, using a K-block reduction over the intermediate dim to stream partial outputs directly into y. Because F is a reduction dim, this fusion is a producer-consumer along a shared iteration space.

Do not fuse anything: three separate kernel launches (up GEMM, activation, down GEMM) let each op run its optimal tile shape and give the profiler cleaner boundaries; fusion of any pair uniformly slows the block due to register pressure.

Fuse up + down into a single kernel by concatenating W_up and W_down^T into one weight matrix, then apply the activation last. This yields one GEMM with concatenated weights and one final elementwise activation.

assumptions: F > D so the intermediate [B, N, F] is larger than the input/output.
Standard elementwise activation (GELU/SiLU) that is cheap per element.

questions.subtopic: Fused kernels / Benefits and boundary conditions
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish real benefits and non-benefits of kernel fusion for transformer building blocks.
questions.stem: Select all correct statements about kernel fusion in transformer inference. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: Kernel fusion always improves latency because it eliminates all HBM traffic between the fused ops; there is no configuration in which fusion hurts performance.
Aggressive fusion can hurt occupancy by inflating per-thread register footprint; when register pressure spills to local memory, the fused kernel may be slower than the un-fused version.
Fusion primarily reduces HBM roundtrips of intermediate tensors and amortizes kernel-launch overhead; the FLOP count of the fused operations is unchanged.

Producer-consumer fusion (e.g., pointwise ops on the output of a GEMM) is straightforward, but fusing across a reduction boundary (e.g., across softmax) requires restructuring the tiling and typically only pays off under specific tile-size constraints.

assumptions: 'Fusion' means combining multiple logical ops into a single kernel launch.
GPU with register file and SMEM as the on-chip staging levels.

questions.subtopic: Fused QKV projection / GEMM merging
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the three Q, K, V linear projections are fused into a single GEMM and what the correctness and performance requirements are.
questions.stem: A transformer implementation replaces three separate linear projections (X@W_Q, X@W_K, X@W_V) with a single fused GEMM X @ [W_Q | W_K | W_V] whose output is sliced into Q, K, V. Which characterization is correct?

options.text: Fusing the three projections produces different Q, K, V values compared to separate projections because the shared reduction accumulator introduces cross-projection numerical coupling; the fusion must be disabled whenever bit-exact reproducibility of separate projections is required.
Fused QKV is only safe when H_kv = H (i.e., MHA); MQA and GQA break the fusion because Q has H heads while K, V have H_kv < H heads, so the concatenated weight matrix is no longer rectangular.

The fusion doubles compute FLOPs because the combined weight matrix is [D, 3D] rather than [D, D], turning the projection into a wider GEMM whose runtime is bounded by tensor-core issue rate rather than memory.

Numerically the fused and separate projections are equivalent (up to rounding order). The primary benefit is a single kernel launch and one HBM read of X instead of three; the concatenation of the weight matrices is done offline so W is fetched once for the combined GEMM.

assumptions: Weights are stored contiguously as a single [D, 3D] (or [D, D + 2*H_kv*d]) tensor.
The output is contiguous and can be sliced without copies.

questions.subtopic: GEMM / Tile size and shared-memory reuse
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the arithmetic intensity of a tiled GEMM kernel and why larger tiles increase compute-per-byte until register/SMEM pressure caps the design.

requiredFeatures: sufficient register file for M_TILE x N_TILE accumulators

questions.stem: A tiled GEMM kernel uses per-thread-block tiles M_TILE x N_TILE with a K-loop step of K_TILE, staging A and B fragments in shared memory. Which statement about arithmetic intensity is correct?

options.text: Arithmetic intensity is independent of M_TILE and N_TILE because each output element ultimately requires exactly 2K flops and 2K element reads regardless of tiling; tile sizing only affects launch grid dimensions, not HBM traffic per output.

Arithmetic intensity scales with K_TILE, not with M_TILE/N_TILE, because A and B are streamed along K; therefore choosing K_TILE = K (full K in one step) is always optimal for HBM traffic minimization.

Increasing M_TILE and N_TILE raises arithmetic intensity roughly as (M_TILE*N_TILE)/(M_TILE+N_TILE), so larger tiles amortize each fetched A/B row/column over more MACs; the ceiling is set by register/SMEM capacity per SM.

Because the C accumulator is written once at the end, HBM write traffic dominates and arithmetic intensity is determined by the M_TILE*N_TILE / (M_TILE*N_TILE*sizeof(C)) ratio, so increasing tile size reduces intensity.

assumptions: M, N, K are large enough that boundary effects are negligible.
A and B are fetched from HBM (no L2 residency guarantees).

questions.subtopic: GEMV / Memory-bound characterization
questions.learningObjective: Explain why GEMV is memory-bound on GPU and how per-row parallelism does not change its roofline classification.
questions.stem: For y = A @ x where A is [M, N] and x is [N], both FP16, what is the correct classification of a well-implemented GEMV on modern GPUs, and why?

options.text: Memory-bound: each output element reuses x lightly (N reads) but A is streamed with essentially no reuse, so intensity is ≈ 1 flop/byte for FP16, well below the ridge point of modern GPUs; runtime is dominated by HBM bandwidth of A.
Compute-bound when N is large: as N grows, the intensity per output row grows linearly with N, so long inner dimensions push GEMV into the compute-limited regime regardless of dtype or memory system.

Compute-bound: GEMV performs 2*M*N flops with M*N loads, giving arithmetic intensity of about 2 flops/byte for FP16, which sits comfortably above modern GPU ridge points and therefore saturates tensor-core throughput.

Latency-bound: the reduction across N introduces a long serial dependency chain on each output row, and this dependency, not memory or compute, determines runtime on modern out-of-order GPU pipelines.

assumptions: A is not cache-resident (M*N is much larger than L2).
The kernel uses efficient row-parallel decomposition with warp-shuffle reductions.

questions.subtopic: Grouped GEMM / MoE batched execution
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a Grouped GEMM is and why it is preferred over per-expert independent GEMMs in sparse MoE serving.
questions.stem: In a sparse MoE layer with E experts, after routing each expert i receives n_i tokens (n_i variable, sum n_i = k * B * N). Which choice best describes Grouped GEMM and why it is used?

options.text: Grouped GEMM is a Winograd-like transform that combines groups of adjacent experts into a shared linear operator; only the transform + inverse-transform cost per group scales with n_i, so the algorithm reduces FLOPs by a factor of E.

Grouped GEMM sums the outputs of E GEMMs into a single [B*N, F] tensor as part of the same kernel; the 'grouping' refers to the reduction across experts, and the kernel is chosen because it fuses the final combination step of MoE.

Grouped GEMM pads all n_i to the same length n_max and runs a single batched GEMM [E, n_max, F]. It is preferred because a single batched GEMM primitive is always faster than a grouped kernel; the padding overhead is negligible.

Grouped GEMM executes E GEMMs of shapes [n_i, D] x [D, F] as a single kernel launch that dispatches per-group tile schedules across SMs. Compared to E independent GEMM launches, it amortizes launch overhead and lets small n_i groups share SMs with larger groups, avoiding SM under-utilization on skinny GEMMs.

assumptions: Token distribution across experts is variable and often skewed.
Modern CUTLASS or cuBLAS grouped-GEMM APIs are available.

questions.subtopic: GQA / Compute vs memory trade-off across variants
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish how MQA/GQA affect KV memory, decode compute, and quality relative to MHA.
questions.stem: Select all statements that are correct about GQA (Grouped Query Attention) relative to MHA and MQA. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: GQA is typically found to preserve model quality better than MQA, at the cost of using more KV memory than MQA but still much less than MHA.

GQA cannot be applied to a pretrained MHA model without full retraining, because the arrangement of KV heads is a topological property of the attention operator that is not amenable to post-hoc adaptation.
GQA reduces per-token KV cache to 2 * G * d per layer (G = number of KV groups), which for typical G = H/8 or H/4 gives 4-8x KV footprint reduction over MHA.
GQA reduces total attention FLOPs at inference by the same factor as it reduces KV heads, because each query head only needs to compute attention against a subset of KV heads.

assumptions: G divides H evenly; each group of H/G query heads shares one KV head.
Discussion is inference decode compute/memory, not training.

questions.subtopic: KV Cache / Read-write pattern in prefill vs decode
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the KV cache read/write pattern in prefill vs decode and characterize the resulting HBM traffic per token.
questions.stem: Consider a decoder-only transformer running (a) prefill on an input of length P, then (b) autoregressive decode for T new tokens. For a single attention layer with H_kv KV heads and head dim d, which characterization of KV cache HBM traffic is correct?

options.text: Prefill writes P tokens' KV once (O(P * H_kv * d)) and reads nothing; decode reads the growing cache once per step but does not write, so total KV bandwidth is O(P * H_kv * d + T * (P+T) * H_kv * d / 2) roughly.

Prefill and decode both write and read the entire KV cache every step: prefill because each token attends to all previous tokens, and decode because each step re-verifies previously written entries. Total KV bandwidth is O((P+T)^2 * H_kv * d).

KV cache is never touched in decode; decode only recomputes K and V from the current token and multiplies by all previous Q vectors that are re-read from HBM. Total KV bandwidth is therefore O(T * H_kv * d).

Prefill writes each of the P tokens' KV once and reads the growing cache for the causal attention (roughly O(P^2 * H_kv * d) reads inside a FlashAttention-style kernel this collapses to O(P^2 d / M) HBM). Decode writes exactly 1 new KV entry per step and reads the entire current cache (P + t) each step, giving read traffic Σ_{t=1..T} (P+t) * H_kv * d ≈ O(T*(P+T) * H_kv * d).

assumptions: Standard causal decoder attention (each token attends to all earlier positions including itself).
KV cache is a monotonically growing tensor; entries are written once and never overwritten (except on preemption).

questions.subtopic: KV cache dataflow / Layout and bandwidth
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the KV cache dataflow during a single autoregressive decode step and its interaction with attention kernels.
questions.stem: Consider one decode step for a batch of B sequences, each of length seq_len (varying). Select all correct statements about KV-cache dataflow inside a single attention layer. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: Because decode is memory-bandwidth bound on KV reads, KV cache quantization (e.g., FP8 or INT8 KV) is a direct lever on decode latency, subject to available dequant kernels and acceptable accuracy loss.

The step writes exactly one new K entry and one new V entry per sequence (each of size H_kv * d), then reads the full cache of length seq_len for each sequence to compute attention. Write traffic is small; read traffic is dominated by seq_len.

KV cache must be stored in one contiguous [B, H_kv, MAX_SEQ, d] tensor per layer to enable coalesced reads by the attention kernel; PagedAttention breaks this requirement and therefore has strictly higher HBM latency per attention step.

In MQA/GQA the same K, V pair is read by multiple query heads within a token; a well-designed attention kernel keeps the loaded K/V tile in SMEM and reuses it across query heads, avoiding redundant HBM reads.

assumptions: Sequences of varying length are handled either as a batched-with-mask kernel or via a paged attention kernel.
Standard decoder-only causal attention.

questions.subtopic: MHA vs MQA vs GQA / KV cache footprint
questions.learningObjective: Compare per-token KV-cache footprint of MHA, MQA, and GQA and its effect on decode-time HBM traffic.
questions.stem: A transformer has H query heads and head dim d. Which comparison of per-token KV-cache size and decode-time HBM traffic is correct? (K and V each contribute one head dim per KV head.)

options.text: MHA, MQA, and GQA all use H_kv = H; they only differ in how the QK^T scores are shared across heads at the software level and therefore have identical KV footprint per token. The performance difference is entirely due to different attention kernels.

MHA has H_kv = H, so per-token KV footprint (K+V) is 2*H*d elements per layer; MQA has H_kv = 1 (2*d per layer); GQA has 1 < H_kv < H (2*H_kv*d per layer). Decode-time HBM traffic is dominated by streaming KV each step, so MQA cuts KV bandwidth by a factor of H relative to MHA and GQA sits between MQA and MHA.

MHA has H_kv = 1 (one shared K, V), MQA has H_kv = H, and GQA has H_kv in between. The naming follows 'multi' for the multi-headed K/V design in MHA and 'multi-query' for the multi-headed Q design in MQA.
MQA halves KV cache versus MHA (H_kv = H/2) and GQA halves it again (H_kv = H/4); both are fixed ratios and independent of the number of query heads.

assumptions: Discussion is about the KV cache of a decoder-only transformer at inference; per-token cache excludes Q since Q is not cached.
GQA uses H_kv = G groups; each group of query heads shares one K and one V head.

questions.subtopic: MoE / Compute, parameter, and imbalance properties
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish correct claims about MoE compute/parameter efficiency and imbalance from common misconceptions.
questions.stem: A top-2 MoE model with E=8 experts replaces a dense FFN block. Select all correct statements. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: MoE inference is always memory-bandwidth bound because every forward pass must load all E experts' weights from HBM; expert parallelism does not help because it only distributes the weight-loading cost, not the parameter footprint.

The total parameter count scales linearly with E (all E experts have their own weight matrices), and the compute per token scales with E as well because the router must compute a gating score against every expert.
Total parameter count scales linearly with E, but compute per token is roughly constant in E (top-k activated) plus a small O(E) gating cost. This is why MoE gives parameter-to-flop leverage.

In serving, load imbalance across experts is a real problem: with random routing the variance of tokens-per-expert scales as sqrt(B*N/E), which can cause hot experts to bottleneck the batched matmul. Capacity limits or expert-parallel load-balancing are needed.

assumptions: Top-k MoE with k << E.
Routing is roughly balanced under normal training; imbalance is a corner case, not the norm.

questions.subtopic: MoE / Top-k routing and dispatch
questions.learningObjective: Describe the MoE routing pipeline: gating, top-k expert selection, and token dispatch to experts.
questions.stem: In a top-k MoE MLP layer with E experts, each token is routed to k experts based on a gating network. Which description of the dataflow is correct?

options.text: The gate produces scores over the E experts per token; top-k experts (typically k=2) are selected and each token contributes to those k experts' input batches with weights = softmax over the top-k scores. Only the k selected experts run their MLP on that token, and outputs are combined by the gate weights. Load balancing across experts is enforced by auxiliary losses / capacity limits.

The gating network selects a single expert per token; multi-expert (top-k > 1) MoE always requires k independent forward passes through the full MLP block, because token-to-expert routing is not amenable to batched execution.

The gate produces per-expert probabilities for each token; every token is routed to the expert with highest probability, and its output is scaled by that probability. The scaling is what preserves gradient flow through the routing decision.

Every token is sent to every expert; the gating scores are used only as a soft mask on the outputs so that experts with score 0 contribute nothing. The 'sparsity' of MoE is entirely about the sum of gating weights, not about avoided compute.

assumptions: Discussion is of top-k sparse MoE at inference or training, not dense mixture.
Capacity limits and drop policies are implementation details not affecting the routing definition.

questions.subtopic: Online Softmax / One-pass streaming reduction
questions.learningObjective: State the online softmax update rules that let a single-pass streaming algorithm compute exact softmax over a partitioned row.
questions.stem: An online softmax algorithm streams over a row in tiles B_1, B_2, .... After processing tile B_t it maintains a running max m_t and a running denominator d_t such that d_t = sum_{i in B_1..t} exp(x_i - m_t). Which update rule is correct when a new tile B_{t+1} arrives with local max m' and local denominator d' = sum_{i in B_{t+1}} exp(x_i - m')?
questions.codeSnippet:
# State after tile t:  m_t (running max), d_t = sum_{i<=t} exp(x_i - m_t)
# New tile stats:      m' = max over B_{t+1};   d' = sum_{i in B_{t+1}} exp(x_i - m')
# We want:             m_{t+1} = max(m_t, m'),  d_{t+1} = sum_{i<=t+1} exp(x_i - m_{t+1})

options.text: m_{t+1} = max(m_t, m') ; d_{t+1} = d_t * exp(m_t - m_{t+1}) + d' * exp(m' - m_{t+1})  (both partial denominators are rescaled by the exponential of the difference between their old reference max and the new global max.)
m_{t+1} = max(m_t, m') ; d_{t+1} = d_t + d'  (the max is the elementwise maximum; the denominator combines by simple addition because both partial sums are already normalized.)

m_{t+1} = max(m_t, m') ; d_{t+1} = d_t + d' * exp(m' - m_{t+1})  (only the new tile's denominator needs a correction factor because the old running sum was already normalized to the true maximum seen so far.)
m_{t+1} = m_t + m' ; d_{t+1} = d_t + d'  (sum both running max and denominator to preserve the streaming invariant.)

assumptions: All exp arguments (x_i - m_{t+1}) are non-positive so no overflow.
Sufficient accumulation precision (typically FP32).

questions.subtopic: Reduction / Warp shuffle vs shared-memory tree
questions.learningObjective: Compare warp-shuffle intra-warp reductions with shared-memory tree reductions for a per-block sum.
questions.stem: A CUDA kernel needs to sum an array of length N per thread block (block size 256, 8 warps of 32 threads). Which implementation strategy is standard and correct?

options.text: Strategy Y is preferred: shared-memory tree with __syncthreads() barriers is the most portable and typically fastest option because it avoids shuffle latency, and the cost of 8 barriers is amortized over N reads.

Strategy X is preferred: __shfl_down_sync reduces within a warp in log2(32) = 5 cycles without SMEM or barriers, then the 8 warp-level partial sums are written to SMEM and reduced by one warp with another shuffle. This is the standard 'warp-shuffle + shared' pattern and is faster than a pure SMEM tree.

Strategy Z (atomicAdd from every thread) is preferred: modern GPUs have hardware-level atomic aggregation that makes this the fastest path; it also avoids the need for shared memory and barriers entirely.
All three strategies produce bit-identical results in FP32 because the number of additions is the same; the choice is purely stylistic and has no measurable performance impact.

assumptions: Reduction is over FP32 or integer values; the strategy generalizes to FP16 with FP32 accumulate.
Block size is a multiple of 32 (warpSize).

questions.subtopic: RMSNorm / Kernel structure and non-implications
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish correct claims about RMSNorm's compute pattern from common overgeneralizations.
questions.stem: Select all correct statements about RMSNorm y = x * rsqrt(mean(x^2) + eps) * g. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: RMSNorm is memory-bandwidth bound in practice: for a row of length N, the kernel reads N x-values and 1 weight tensor once, writes N y-values once, and performs O(N) elementwise operations plus one reduction — the reduction and rsqrt are negligible relative to HBM traffic on modern hardware.
RMSNorm requires a single reduction (E[x^2]) over the normalization axis and no mean subtraction; per-element compute is fewer ops than LayerNorm.
RMSNorm is compute-bound on modern GPUs because the rsqrt and elementwise scaling per element are expensive relative to the memory bandwidth used.
RMSNorm is mathematically identical to LayerNorm applied to zero-mean inputs, so it can always be replaced by LayerNorm with the same weights without changing the trained model.

assumptions: Standard implementations with FP32 accumulation.
Weight g is per-feature (one scalar per feature dim).

questions.subtopic: RMSNorm vs LayerNorm / Compute and memory pattern
questions.learningObjective: Compare compute and memory patterns of RMSNorm vs LayerNorm and identify which reduction operations each requires.
questions.stem: Compare a per-row RMSNorm — y = x * rsqrt(mean(x^2) + eps) * g — with LayerNorm — y = (x - mean(x)) / sqrt(var(x) + eps) * g + b. Which comparison of reductions and memory is correct?

options.text: Both require exactly one reduction (over the row); RMSNorm reduces sum(x), LayerNorm reduces sum(x^2). Total HBM traffic is identical because both read the row once and write the row once.

LayerNorm requires two reductions over the row (mean and variance) that must be executed in two passes; RMSNorm requires two reductions as well (sum of x and sum of x^2) because rsqrt needs both statistics.

RMSNorm needs one reduction (sum of x^2); LayerNorm can be computed with one reduction (using E[x^2] - E[x]^2) but requires two moments (sum and sum of squares). HBM read of x is once per row in both; RMSNorm skips the mean subtraction and the bias b, giving fewer per-element ops.
RMSNorm requires two passes over x (one to compute mean(x^2), one to normalize); LayerNorm is single-pass because the numerator can subsume the mean in a running formula.

assumptions: The full row fits in one program's registers / SMEM for a single-pass implementation; if not, an online algorithm is needed.
eps is a positive scalar to avoid division by zero.

questions.subtopic: RoPE / Rotary position embedding computation
questions.learningObjective: Explain the elementwise rotation pattern of RoPE and where in the transformer stack it is applied.
questions.stem: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is applied to Q and K in an attention layer. Which characterization of RoPE's computation and dataflow is correct?

options.text: RoPE is applied to the attention scores QK^T by adding a bias matrix whose entry (i, j) is a function of the relative position i - j; the scores are then softmaxed. Q and K themselves are unchanged.

RoPE is added elementwise to Q, K, and V as a learned position embedding table indexed by position; the addition happens after the softmax so that the rotation applies to the attention weights themselves rather than to the projections.

RoPE rotates pairs of feature dimensions of Q and K by position-dependent angles theta_{pos, i}; it is applied elementwise to Q and K after the QKV projection but before the QK^T score computation. RoPE is not applied to V, and each token's rotation is independent of other tokens.

RoPE is a data-dependent low-rank correction applied to Q, K, V that requires a full reduction over the sequence dimension per token; this reduction is the reason RoPE is expensive to compute in decode.

assumptions: Standard RoPE as in RoFormer / Llama; extensions (linear/NTK scaling) modify the frequency schedule but not the rotation structure.
d is even so features can be paired.

questions.subtopic: Sampling / Temperature and top-p (nucleus)
questions.learningObjective: Explain what temperature and top-p sampling do at the logits/probability level.
questions.stem: Which description of temperature (T) and top-p (nucleus, p) sampling for LLM decoding is correct?

options.text: Temperature T scales the logits by exp(T) after softmax; top-p sorts the resulting probabilities in ascending order and keeps the first p fraction of the distribution, then renormalizes.

Temperature T divides the logits by T before the softmax (T > 1 flattens the distribution, T < 1 sharpens it); top-p, after softmax, sorts probabilities in descending order and keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability first exceeds p, then renormalizes over this set before sampling.
Temperature T divides the softmax output by T; top-p keeps exactly floor(p * V) tokens by count (not by cumulative probability) to give an upper bound on the sampling set size.
Temperature T is applied by clipping logits above the T-th percentile; top-p is a synonym for top-k with p = k / V, so the two are algebraically equivalent under this identification.

assumptions: T > 0 (strictly positive).

questions.subtopic: Softmax / Numerical stability via max subtraction
questions.learningObjective: Explain why row-max subtraction is required for a numerically stable softmax and what happens when it is omitted.
questions.stem: The 'safe softmax' formulation is softmax(x)_i = exp(x_i - m) / sum_j exp(x_j - m) where m = max_j x_j. Which statement about this formulation is correct?
questions.codeSnippet:
# Naive softmax
# y_i = exp(x_i) / sum_j exp(x_j)

# Safe softmax
# m   = max_j x_j
# e_i = exp(x_i - m)          # e_i in (0, 1]
# y_i = e_i / sum_j e_j

options.text: Subtracting m makes every exponent non-positive so exp(x_i - m) lies in (0, 1], preventing overflow when any x_i is large; the algebraic identity softmax(x) = softmax(x - c) for any constant c guarantees the result is unchanged in exact arithmetic.

The subtraction shifts the outputs by exp(-m) but this factor cancels in the ratio, so mathematically both forms are equivalent and safe softmax is only needed on integer hardware without native FP exponent range.

The main benefit of max subtraction is preventing underflow of the denominator; overflow of individual exp(x_i) is already handled by IEEE-754 saturation to inf which cancels in the division and yields the correct value.

Max subtraction changes softmax outputs by a constant additive offset; this offset is absorbed by the following LayerNorm in transformer stacks, so safe softmax and naive softmax produce identical logits at the final output only in the presence of a downstream normalization.

assumptions: Inputs are finite floats; NaN inputs are not addressed by max subtraction.
The reduction uses appropriate precision (typically FP32 accumulate).

questions.subtopic: Sparse vs dense kernel boundary / When sparsity pays
questions.learningObjective: Identify when unstructured or structured sparsity actually reduces wall-clock time on GPU, vs when it only reduces FLOP count.

hardwareContext.architecture: Ampere or newer for 2:4 sparse tensor cores

questions.stem: Select all statements that correctly characterize the boundary between sparse and dense GPU kernels. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: Any percentage of sparsity greater than 50% in a weight matrix automatically gives a proportional wall-clock speedup on modern GPUs, since sparse tensor-cores dynamically skip zero tiles regardless of the sparsity pattern.

Unstructured sparsity (arbitrary zero pattern) rarely translates to wall-clock speedup on GPU unless density is well below ~10%, because indexing overhead and irregular memory access outweigh the FLOP reduction on tensor-core-driven dense hardware.

Structured 2:4 sparsity (Ampere) preserves tensor-core throughput at half the FLOP cost of the equivalent dense GEMM; it is a hardware-native format supported by cuSPARSELt / cuBLAS sparse APIs and yields real speedup on supported dtypes.

For LLM inference, weight sparsity that reduces HBM traffic (e.g., N:M or block-sparse weight formats) is more impactful than FLOP reduction, because decode is bandwidth-bound. However, this only works if a compatible sparse kernel exists for the target dtype.

assumptions: GPU refers to modern NVIDIA GPUs (Ampere and newer).
'Sparse kernel' means a specialized kernel that reads only nonzeros and their indices.

questions.subtopic: SwiGLU MLP / Parameter count and compute
questions.learningObjective: Characterize the SwiGLU MLP block: three linear layers with a gated activation and its parameter/compute compared to a standard two-linear MLP.
questions.stem: The SwiGLU MLP block used in Llama-style LLMs computes y = (silu(x @ W_gate) * (x @ W_up)) @ W_down where W_gate, W_up are [D, F] and W_down is [F, D]. Which characterization is correct?

options.text: SwiGLU has three linear layers (gate, up, down) — 3 * D * F parameters vs 2 * D * F for a standard two-linear MLP at intermediate dim F. To keep parameter/FLOP budget constant when moving from a GELU MLP with intermediate dim F to SwiGLU, implementations typically use SwiGLU with intermediate dim (2/3) * F.

SwiGLU is equivalent to a GELU MLP with intermediate dim F, but requires an extra elementwise multiplication that raises per-token FLOPs by 50% compared to a two-linear MLP with the same F; parameter count is the same.

SwiGLU uses three linear layers (gate, up, down), which triples both parameters and FLOPs relative to a standard two-linear MLP at the same intermediate dim F; to keep parameter budget constant, implementations must halve F when switching from GELU to SwiGLU.

SwiGLU is a bilinear activation between x @ W_gate and x @ W_up; the elementwise product of these two projections replaces the ReLU/GELU nonlinearity but does not increase parameter count over a standard MLP because the gate and up projections share weights via a symmetry constraint.

assumptions: The comparison baseline is a two-linear GELU MLP: up [D, F] and down [F, D].
silu(x) = x * sigmoid(x) is the elementwise nonlinearity on the gate branch.

questions.subtopic: Top-k / Sampling primitive on GPU
questions.learningObjective: Explain the standard GPU strategy for computing top-k over a large vocabulary and why full sort is not required.
questions.stem: An LLM sampler needs to compute the top-k tokens per batch row over a [B, V] logits tensor, where V is typically 32K-200K and k is small (e.g. 50). Which GPU strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Use a two-stage approach: partition each row into blocks, keep a per-block top-k with a small in-register heap or bitonic-select, then merge the per-block candidates into a single top-k with a final reduction. Total work is O(V log k), well below full-sort.

Sort each row in full with a merge sort or radix sort of complexity O(V log V), then take the top k. This is essentially the only correct approach because partial-selection algorithms cannot guarantee stable order among ties.
Compute softmax over the entire row and then threshold at 1 / (k * V); this yields top-k without any sort because the probability of the k-th largest logit is bounded above by 1/k in expectation.
Top-k is inherently sequential across the V dimension because each selection depends on all previous ones; the only GPU-friendly path is to move top-k to the CPU on a small logits copy over PCIe.

assumptions: V is much larger than k so partitioning is beneficial.
Ties can be resolved with an arbitrary stable rule (e.g., lower index wins).
